transcript.text: The Linux file system is a hierarchical tree rooted at the forward slash directory containing every file and directory on the system including devices configuration and user home directories.
The ls command lists directory contents and with the hyphen la flag shows all files including hidden dot files along with their permissions owner group size and modification time.
File permissions appear as a ten character string the first character shows the file type a dash for regular file and the letter d for a directory entry in the filesystem.
The next nine characters form three groups of three representing read write and execute permissions for three classes of user the owner the group members and everyone else.
chmod changes permissions using symbolic mode like chmod u plus x to add execute permission for the owner or numeric octal mode like chmod 755 to set all three classes at once.
In octal mode each digit is a sum of four for read two for write and one for execute so 755 means rwx for owner and rx for group and others.
The pipe operator represented by a vertical bar character connects two commands so the standard output of the left command becomes the standard input of the right command.
grep filters lines from its input that match a given pattern and when combined with pipes allows you to search and filter the output of any command efficiently.
Redirection operators change where output goes the single greater than sign redirects standard output to a file and overwrites any existing content in that file.
Two greater than signs append output to a file without overwriting existing content and the less than sign redirects a file as standard input to a command.
Understanding pipes and redirection together lets you build command pipelines combining grep sort uniq cut and other tools to process data entirely from the command line.
Shell scripting captures these pipelines in reusable scripts with variables loops and conditionals making automation and batch processing straightforward on any Linux system.
Environment variables store configuration values that shell commands and scripts can read the PATH variable for example lists directories the shell searches for executable files.
Process management commands like ps show running processes and kill sends signals to terminate or pause them while top provides a real time view of resource usage.
Combining all these tools with man pages for documentation and tab completion for discovery makes the Linux command line a powerful environment for professional developers and administrators.
Practice these fundamentals by writing small scripts that use pipes redirection and permission management and your confidence on the command line will grow quickly.
